mainTopic: Whether חכמים disagree with רבי אליעזר בן יעקב about נדרי זירוזין (vows said only to pressure someone), using the משנה about a vow made to push a friend to accept a gift for his son.
overview: The גמרא quotes a משנה: someone vows not to benefit from his friend unless the friend accepts a gift for his son, and the friend can cancel the vow without a חכם by saying, 'Not taking it is my honor.' The גמרא infers that without this claim the vow would bind. That seems to go against רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, who holds that נדרי זירוזין (vows said only to pressure someone) do not count, so it seems the רבנן disagree with him. The גמרא answers that he agrees this vow is real, because the vower means it: 'I'm not a dog who only takes.' The same pattern repeats with the reverse case of רבי מאיר and חכמים, and the answer there is 'I'm not a king who only gives.' מר קשישא then tries a third proof from the משנה of נדרי אונסין, about a vow to come eat at a friend's meal. רב אשי answers that there the guest made the host vow, so it was a real promise and not pressure. Finally the גמרא brings a ברייתא where רבי אליעזר בן יעקב adds a case of hospitality vows and 'the חכמים did not agree with him.' The גמרא begins asking what exactly they rejected, and the answer comes on the next עמוד.

steps.title: A vow to make a friend accept a gift for his son
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה. Someone vows not to benefit from his friend unless the friend accepts a gift for his son. The friend can cancel the vow without a חכם by saying that refusing is his honor.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says, 'Benefiting from you is קונם for me if you don't take a כור of wheat and two barrels of wine for your son,' the friend can cancel the vow without a חכם. He can say: 'You only said this for my honor, and this (not taking) is my honor.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting a משנה about a vow made to push a friend into accepting a generous gift. This is the base text the next steps will analyze.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The one vowing wanted to honor his friend by giving his son a gift. The friend says that his honor is actually better served by not taking anything. Since the vow's whole purpose has been 'fulfilled' in another way, no חכם is needed to release it.

keyTerms.meaning: A word used to make a vow, like saying 'this is forbidden to me like a קרבן'
A large measure of grain
To release or cancel his vow
Without going to a Torah scholar for release
My honor

if you do not take for your son

phrases.english: a kor of wheat and two barrels of wine"

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow made to pressure a friend into accepting a gift can be released by the friend without a חכם, because he can say that refusing is his honor.

steps.title: Inferring that the רבנן disagree with רבי אליעזר בן יעקב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers from the משנה that without the claim 'this is my honor,' the vow would be binding. Under רבי אליעזר בן יעקב it should be a non-binding נדרי זירוזין, so it seems the רבנן disagree with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason is only because he said 'this is my honor.' Otherwise, it would be a real vow. Whose view is this? If it were רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, this would be a vow of urging, which doesn't count. So learn from here that the רבנן disagree with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads a hidden implication out of the משנה and uses it to prove that the רבנן argue with רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה needed a special argument ('this is my honor') to cancel the vow. That shows that, on its own, the vow counts. But a vow said only to push someone should be a non-binding נדרי זירוזין. So the author of this משנה must be the רבנן, who treat such vows as real.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason is (used to make an inference)
But if it were not so
Whose opinion is this?
Vows of urging, said only to pressure someone and not meant as real vows
Learn from this
They disagree

phrases.english: The reason is that he said "this is my honor"
but if not so, it is a vow.
Whose view is this?
If it is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov,
it is a vow of urging.
phrases.notes: A 'vow of urging' is just pressure on the other person, so it does not really count as a vow.

phrases.english: Rather, learn from this:
the Rabbis disagree with him.

steps.triggerLanguage: טעמא דאמר זה הוא כבודי הא לאו הכי נדר הוא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from the משנה just quoted.
steps.raayaObject: That the רבנן disagree with רבי אליעזר בן יעקב and treat נדרי זירוזין as binding vows.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's need for the 'this is my honor' argument, which implies the vow would otherwise count.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב admits this case is a real vow
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The משנה can follow רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, because in this case the person really means the vow. He doesn't want to be someone who only takes and never gives.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, it is רבי אליעזר בן יעקב. He agrees that this is a real vow, because the person is saying: 'I am not a dog, that I benefit from you and you don't benefit from me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof. It shows that this case is different from an ordinary vow of urging.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A vow of urging is only pressure. Here, the one vowing truly means it, because he refuses to keep taking from his friend without giving back. So even רבי אליעזר בן יעקב treats it as a real vow, and nothing is proven about the רבנן.

keyTerms.meaning: Actually, really (used to keep the original attribution)
And he agrees / admits
A dog
I benefit

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבי אליעזר בן יעקב changed his general rule. He still holds that vows of urging don't count. This case just isn't a vow of urging, because the person sincerely means it.

phrases.aramaic: לְעוֹלָם רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב הִיא,
phrases.english: Actually, it is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov,
and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov agrees
in this case that it is a vow,
because he is saying to him:
I am not a dog,
that I benefit from you

steps.triggerLanguage: לעולם רבי אליעזר בן יעקב היא ומודה רבי אליעזר בן יעקב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The conclusion that the רבנן disagree with רבי אליעזר בן יעקב cannot be drawn from this משנה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed this case is a vow of urging. In fact the person sincerely means the vow, so it counts even according to רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.

steps.title: A new test: the reverse case with רבי מאיר and חכמים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the next part of the משנה. Someone forbids his friend from benefiting from him unless the friend gives a gift to his son. רבי מאיר says the vow holds until the friend gives. חכמים say the one who vowed can release it by saying, 'It's as if I received it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if someone says to his friend, 'Benefiting from me is קונם for you unless you give my son a כור of wheat and two barrels of wine,' רבי מאיר says the vow holds until he gives. חכמים say this person, too, can cancel his vow without a חכם, because he can say: 'I consider it as if I received it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new attempt to settle the question by quoting the continuation of the משנה. This step sets up the next move in the discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the roles are reversed: the one vowing wants to receive, not give. רבי מאיר treats the vow as binding until the gift is given. חכמים let the one who vowed drop his demand himself. The גמרא will now examine what this dispute shows about vows of urging.

keyTerms.meaning: Until he gives
I consider it as if I received it

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One who says to his friend
"Konam that you benefit from me
if you do not give my son

phrases.aramaic: כּוֹר שֶׁל חִיטִּין וּשְׁתֵּי חָבִיּוֹת שֶׁל יַיִן״,
phrases.english: a kor of wheat and two barrels of wine"
Rabbi Meir says: until he gives.
phrases.notes: He means the friend stays forbidden to benefit until he actually gives the gift.

phrases.english: And the Sages say:

phrases.aramaic: אַף זֶה יָכוֹל לְהַתִּיר אֶת נִדְרוֹ

without a sage,
because he can say:

steps.triggerLanguage: תא שמע האומר לחבירו קונם שאתה נהנית לי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof was rejected, the גמרא brings the next case in the same משנה to try again.
steps.raayaObject: Whether the רבנן disagree with רבי אליעזר בן יעקב about vows of urging.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The continuation of the משנה: the dispute between רבי מאיר and חכמים in the reverse case.

steps.title: Inference from the חכמים: without 'as if I received it,' the vow would bind
steps.stepSummary: From the חכמים's ruling, the גמרא infers that the vow is normally binding. That seems to go against רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, so it looks like the רבנן disagree with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The only reason he can release the vow is that he says, 'It's as if I received it.' Without that, it would be a real vow. Whose view is this? If it were רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, this would be a vow of urging, which doesn't bind. So it must be the רבנן, and they disagree with him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a proof from the part of the משנה quoted in Step 4. It argues that the חכמים treat this vow as binding, so they must disagree with רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים needed a special release ('it's as if I received it'). That means the vow, on its own, really binds. But under רבי אליעזר בן יעקב a pressuring vow like this should never bind in the first place, so the משנה seems to follow the opposing רבנן.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason (the גמרא points to a detail in order to infer its opposite)
But if it were not so
Vows of urging: vows said only to pressure someone, not really meant
And they disagree

but if not so,
it is a vow.

If it is Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov,
it is a vow of urging (and it would not bind),
rather, is it not the Rabbis, and they disagree!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the proof that Step 4 set up by quoting the משנה
steps.raayaObject: That the רבנן disagree with רבי אליעזר בן יעקב about נדרי זירוזין
steps.raayaSupportSource: The חכמים's need for the release 'הריני כאילו התקבלתי' implies the vow normally binds

steps.title: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב agrees here: 'I am not a king'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. Even רבי אליעזר בן יעקב admits this vow is real, because the vower insists on getting something back for what he gives.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it really can follow רבי אליעזר בן יעקב. He agrees that this one is a real vow, because the man is saying: 'I am not a king, that I give to you and you don't give to me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof. This vow is not just pressure; the person truly means it, so even רבי אליעזר בן יעקב would call it binding.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's rule only covers vows that were never really meant. Here the vower truly wants a two-way relationship and refuses to be a one-sided giver. So the case falls outside his rule, and the proof that the רבנן disagree falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: Actually / really (it can still follow the first opinion)
And he agrees (in this specific case)
A king

phrases.english: No, actually it is Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov,
and Rabbi Eliezer agrees in this case
that it is a vow,
because he says to him:
I am not a king,

phrases.english: that I benefit you

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, לְעוֹלָם רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Full rejection: the משנה can follow רבי אליעזר בן יעקב
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed this was a pressuring vow. In fact the vower truly means it, so it is outside רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's rule.

steps.title: מר קשישא's proof from נדרי אונסין
steps.stepSummary: מר קשישא brings a משנה about a vow to eat at a friend's meal that was blocked by sickness or a river. It implies that without such a block the vow would bind, which seems to go against רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר קשישא son of רב חסדא said to רב אשי: Come and hear. 'Vows blocked by things beyond one's control: his friend made a vow about him that he should eat at his place, and then he got sick, or his son got sick, or a river held him back.' So without these, it would be a real vow. Whose view is this? If it were רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, it would be a vow of urging. So it must be the רבנן, and they disagree!
steps.whatsHappening: A new proof is brought from a different משנה. The question is the same: do the רבנן disagree with רבי אליעזר בן יעקב?
steps.deeperAnalysis: An invitation vow sounds like classic pressure: 'You must come eat with me!' Yet the משנה lets it go only because of things beyond his control, like sickness or a river. That suggests that otherwise it would bind, which goes against רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.

keyTerms.meaning: Vows blocked by things beyond one's control
He made a vow concerning him
A river held him back

the son of Rav Chisda, to Rav Ashi:

and he got sick, or his son got sick,

But if not so,
it is a vow.

steps.raayaObject: That the רבנן disagree with רבי אליעזר בן יעקב
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה of נדרי אונסין (27a), which implies the invitation vow binds when nothing blocks it

steps.title: The guest made the host vow, so it was not urging
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that the case is one where the guest made the host vow to invite him. That is not a pressuring vow, so even רבי אליעזר בן יעקב agrees it binds.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, it follows רבי אליעזר בן יעקב. Do you think the host made the guest vow? No, the guest made the host vow. The guest asked, 'Are you inviting me to your meal?' He said, 'Yes.' 'Is this a vow upon you?' And he vowed. Then he got sick, or his son got sick, or a river held him back. These are vows blocked by things beyond his control.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי rejects the proof by redefining the case. The guest is the one who got the host to make the vow, not the other way around.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A vow of urging is when the host pushes a reluctant guest just to be polite. Here the guest asked for the vow, so the host's vow is a real promise and not polite pressure. That is why it binds, except when something beyond his control stops him, and the משנה fits רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.

keyTerms.meaning: The one inviting (the host)
The one invited (the guest)
And do you think...? (introduces a mistaken assumption)

steps.whatToRemember: All three proofs so far that the רבנן disagree with רבי אליעזר בן יעקב were rejected: the gift for the son, the reverse gift case, and the invitation vow. Each case turned out to be a vow the person truly meant, not just pressure. The next step tries a fourth source.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't assume the vow in the משנה was made by the host to push the guest. רב אשי reads it as the guest getting the host to vow, and that changes everything.

and do you think
that the host made a vow about the guest?
No, the guest made the host vow.
He said to him:
Are you inviting me to your meal?
He said to him: Yes.
"Is this a vow upon you?" And he vowed.
phrases.notes: The guest is the one asking for the vow. That is why it's a real promise and not just polite urging.

phrases.english: And then he got sick, or his son got sick,
or a river held him back,
these are vows blocked by things beyond one's control.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְעוֹלָם רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב, וּמִי סָבְרַתְּ דְּאַדְּרֵיהּ מְזַמְּנָא לִזְמִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects מר קשישא's proof from Step 7
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Full rejection: the משנה can follow רבי אליעזר בן יעקב
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the host made the vow to pressure the guest. Really, the guest asked the host to vow, so it was a real promise and not urging.

steps.title: A ברייתא about a host who vows unless his friend stays for a meal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא in which רבי אליעזר בן יעקב adds a new case of a pushing vow, and the חכמים do not agree with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: Going even further, רבי אליעזר בן יעקב said: If someone says to his friend, 'It is קונם for me to benefit from you unless you stay as my guest and eat hot bread and drink a hot drink with me,' and the friend pushes back and refuses, this too is a pushing vow. But the חכמים did not agree with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source, a ברייתא, to test whether the חכמים argue with רבי אליעזר בן יעקב. It quotes his extra case and the line that the חכמים did not agree with him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier proofs were pushed aside, so the גמרא now tries a source that openly says 'the חכמים did not agree.' In this case the host is pressing his friend to accept his hospitality, and רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says it is only a pushing vow. Step 10 asks which part the חכמים rejected.

keyTerms.meaning: Going even further than the earlier case
Staying as a guest
He pushed back against him, refusing the offer
Pushing vows: vows said only to pressure someone, not meant seriously
The חכמים did not agree with him

steps.confusionAlert: Here the vower is the host, pressuring his friend to come and eat. The friend refusing does not make the vow serious in רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's eyes; he sees it as a polite back-and-forth.

steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא has two parts: the earlier basic rule of רבי אליעזר בן יעקב and his extra case here. If the חכמים rejected the basic rule too, that would prove they argue with him on pushing vows in general. The גמרא is about to test that reading.
